title: TNP - 2026-11-27
intro: Welcome to Trending Not Peak for Friday, November 27. Today, inspect a robot's training pipeline, move test files into simulated iPhones, and experiment with silent dictation. You're hearing a synthetic voice, with AI-assisted writing. Find the projects and their sources at trending not peak dot com.
outro: A few places to begin: REKI to inspect robot pretraining pipelines, CSS mixins to reuse grouped style rules, and SimDrop to move simulator test files. Explore the sources at trending not peak dot com. This is Trending Not Peak. Have fun making something useful, and leave a little time to discover how an Amiga thought your interface should behave.

stories.title: Open the pipeline behind a robot action model
stories.script: First up, REKI opens another part of the route from public data to robot actions. Kyutai has released the data-curation and pretraining code behind its two-point-four-billion-parameter vision-language-action model. That means robotics researchers can use REKI to inspect robot pretraining pipelines, including how different kinds of movement become compatible training examples. The team describes a mixture containing nine hundred million frames from robot manipulation, first-person human video and vision-language data. Its code unifies state and action conventions across robot bodies and human hand motions, while supporting vision-language co-training and subtask prediction. The model was already available; this release exposes the machinery that prepares and trains it. Kyutai calls the full pipeline reproducible, although independent reproduction isn't documented here. A useful investigation is to follow one dataset through those conversions. Which differences between two robot bodies get preserved, and which become a shared convention? Those choices are now available to examine in code.
stories.why_now: Kyutai announced the data-curation and pretraining code release November 26, 2026 at 06:40:03-05:00; the repository's news section independently dates that release November 26. At 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00, the announcement had 116 likes, 9 replies and 6334 views. The retrieved repository displayed 46 stars and 5 forks.
stories.why_early: The material change is release of data-curation and pretraining code for an existing 2.4B vision-language-action model. Kyutai describes public-source pretraining data and a reproducible pipeline; independent reproduction, training costs and transfer across unfamiliar robot embodiments remain unestablished. Global saturation is unknown within the configured sources.
stories.watch_next: Independent pipeline reproductions documenting data preparation, compute requirements and the effect of embodiment-conversion choices.

stories.title: Experiment with reusable blocks of native CSS
stories.script: Over in the browser, CSS mixins are getting close enough to shipping that Microsoft's Patrick Brosset has published a hands-on tour. His team is implementing them in Chromium. Unlike a custom property that holds a value, a mixin can hold several declarations and nested rules. Interface developers could use CSS mixins to reuse grouped style rules, such as the positioning and clipping declarations behind visually hidden text. Define the block with the mixin rule, then apply it wherever it's needed. Parameters can have types and defaults, and a button example includes its hover behavior inside the reusable block. This remains experimental: the examples require a recent Chromium browser with Experimental Web Platform features enabled. There's also a sharp little behavior to investigate. Pass more arguments than the mixin declares, and the application does nothing. Build two button variants in a test page, then deliberately supply an extra argument. See whether your debugging tools make that failure understandable.
stories.why_now: Brosset published the first-person implementation account November 25, 2026. Its Lobsters posting at 19:02:17.726-06:00 had 32 points and 3 comments at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00.
stories.why_early: A Chromium implementation-team member reports substantial progress toward shipping native mixins and supplies executable examples. The feature remains behind an experimental flag; stable release timing and cross-browser availability are not established.
stories.watch_next: Stable Chromium availability, implementation progress in other engines and diagnostics for invalid mixin applications.

stories.title: Put running iOS simulators in Finder
stories.script: Closer to the desktop, SimDrop gives running iOS simulators a surprisingly ordinary interface: folders in the Mac's Finder sidebar. Each booted simulator gets its own location, containing a Photos and Videos folder and a Downloads folder corresponding to the Files app. The location appears when the simulator boots and disappears when it shuts down. iOS developers can use SimDrop to move simulator test files, whether that's a photo for an import screen or a JSON fixture for a file-opening workflow. Those locations are also reachable from the terminal, so an existing script can copy a file into the simulator's Downloads directory. The project requires macOS fifteen or later and offers a signed, notarized download alongside its Homebrew installation route. A useful first check is a file your app already knows how to open. Drop it into Downloads, open it through the simulated Files app, then change the fixture and repeat. The sidebar now has a direct job in your testing loop.
stories.why_now: Show HN introduced SimDrop November 26, 2026 at 16:51:38+00:00. It had 44 points and 10 comments at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00. The retrieved repository displayed 42 stars and 1 fork.
stories.why_early: A fresh public introduction supplies a GPL-3.0 Finder integration with concrete booted-simulator folders, terminal access and downloadable builds. Signing and notarization are project descriptions; independent compatibility and file-transfer reliability are unestablished.
stories.watch_next: Independent tests covering multiple booted simulators, file round trips and Photos-library behavior.

stories.title: Design research agents around scientific responsibilities
stories.script: Turning to scientific work, Ai2 has interviewed seventeen scientists about what they'd need before handing research tasks to agents. The resulting report gives tool builders concrete requirements to investigate. Across the interviews, the team identifies five dimensions of trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability and transparency. Think about an agent analyzing a dataset. Researchers need to inspect its methods, understand which files it accessed and reproduce the result. A literature assistant also needs scrutiny for conflicting evidence and claims its citations don't support. Developers building research software could use those questions to shape an experiment record, making the path to an answer inspectable alongside the answer itself. This is a qualitative interview study drawn from an existing researcher network, rather than a representative vote across science. Start with one bounded analysis and ask a colleague to reproduce it from the agent's record. Their first missing detail tells you something useful about the interface you still need to build.
stories.why_now: Ai2 published the primary report November 25, 2026. Its announcement at 13:59:18-05:00 had 24 likes, 3 replies and 2812 views at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00.
stories.why_early: A fresh primary qualitative study translates interviews with 17 scientists into requirements for responsible scientific agents. Participants came through an earlier researcher network. The findings identify design concerns, without establishing representative prevalence or validating a particular safeguard.
stories.watch_next: Research-agent interfaces and evaluations that test reproducibility, access visibility and handling of conflicting evidence.

stories.title: Manage Garage storage through a new web interface
stories.script: Back from the break, Garage two point six adds a web administration interface to the storage project's command-line workflow. The release account describes nearly two years of work on the interface, funded by NLnet. Self-hosters can inspect cluster status, configure its layout, manage buckets and handle access credentials through the browser. That's useful when you're learning the system and want to see how those pieces relate before scripting routine operations. The team supplies a single-node example for trying the release, with a default bucket and an admin token for signing in. One operational detail matters immediately: remote administration over plain HTTP exposes that token, so the project calls for HTTPS or a protected connection such as a VPN. The new interface follows the CLI's organization. Walk through creating a test bucket, then compare the same operation at the command line. That gives you a visual introduction and a path toward repeatable configuration when the experiment grows.
stories.why_now: Garage published its v2.6.0 release account November 25, 2026. Its November 26 Lobsters posting at 06:40:23.353-06:00 had 44 points and 3 comments at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00.
stories.why_early: The meaningful change is a newly released administration UI covering cluster monitoring, layout, buckets and credentials. Garage itself is established. Independent UI reliability and operational experience with this release are not established; the project explicitly identifies transport protection as necessary for remote token use.
stories.watch_next: Independent administration walkthroughs and UI issue reports covering cluster changes and credential management.

stories.title: Turn technical notes into scheduled practice
stories.script: Away from infrastructure, Olumino connects notes with flashcards and a review schedule. Its fresh public introduction presents a Markdown notes and spaced-repetition app, while the current site shows support for highlighted code, mathematical notation and pictures. Developers learning an unfamiliar language could turn a tricky code example into a question, then revisit it after increasing gaps. Olumino uses the FSRS-seven scheduling method, with answers determining when each card returns. Cards forgotten three times in one session move into a separate Revisit area. Teachers can share decks through a class link and inspect study activity and commonly missed cards. The site also lists import and export routes including Anki and Markdown. For a small experiment, make cards from mistakes you've actually made, keeping the explanation beside the code. Check the exported material too. A review schedule becomes more interesting when it brings back the exact misconception that otherwise keeps returning as another debugging session.
stories.why_now: Show HN introduced Olumino November 26, 2026 at 03:33:06+00:00. It had 100 points and 45 comments at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00.
stories.why_early: A fresh public introduction offers a concrete notes-to-flashcards workflow with FSRS-7 scheduling, code and math support, class sharing and documented import/export options. Product-specific learning outcomes and export fidelity are not independently established; spaced repetition itself is established.
stories.watch_next: Independent technical-study examples and round-trip exports preserving code, notation and card structure.

stories.title: Ask a local vision agent which parcel is yours
stories.script: Out among the parcel shelves, Zhaojian gives a small local vision model a very specific assignment: find the package matching your pickup code. You supply the code through text, voice or a message screenshot, then photograph the shelf. The project uses MiniCPM-V four point seven, a one-billion-parameter model running through llama dot cpp on your own computer. Your phone connects over the local network or through a tunnel back to that machine. The agent narrows the search using shelf and level numbers, examines labels, and can crop an area again when a closer view conflicts with its earlier answer. Developers exploring visual assistants get an inspectable example of repeated checking around a physical task. There isn't an independent accuracy result to promise. Begin with a staged shelf of your own labeled boxes, including two easily confused numbers. Watch whether the agent requests a better view and revises its choice when the evidence changes.
stories.why_now: OpenBMB highlighted Zhaojian November 26, 2026 at 07:58:49-05:00. The post had 32 likes, 18 replies and 1002 views at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00. The retrieved MIT-licensed repository displayed 0 stars, 0 forks and 7 commits.
stories.why_early: A newly highlighted challenge project supplies a concrete local MiniCPM-V 4.7 parcel-search agent with iterative visual checking. Local processing and workflow behavior are project descriptions. Independent recognition accuracy, hardware requirements and performance on real pickup shelves remain unestablished.
stories.watch_next: Controlled evaluations with confusing labels, multiple parcels, unreadable images and documented correction behavior.

stories.title: Experiment with silent prompts from webcam lip reading
stories.script: For a quieter interface experiment, lip-dictation lets you mouth a phrase at your webcam and place the recognized words into Claude Code's prompt box. Press a button, silently form the words, then press again to finish. The project runs an Auto-AVSR lip-reading model locally on a Mac and says it records no audio and sends no video off the machine. That gives developers curious about alternative input methods a concrete prototype to inspect. The limitation is central to using it: the author calls accuracy modest, with word errors especially likely on technical terms. You'll need to read the text before sending it. A revealing first comparison is an ordinary sentence followed by one containing a project name and a code identifier. Keep the intended text beside the recognized output. Even a rough result can help you investigate where a confirmation interface needs to make corrections quick, especially when the input itself makes no sound.
stories.why_now: Show HN introduced lip-dictation November 26, 2026 at 14:25:08+00:00. It had 16 points and 2 comments at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00. The retrieved repository displayed 12 stars and 1 fork.
stories.why_early: A fresh MIT-licensed prototype connects local Auto-AVSR visual speech recognition with a Claude Code prompt interface. The author explicitly describes modest accuracy and technical-vocabulary errors. Independent accuracy, accessibility benefits and hardware performance are unestablished.
stories.watch_next: Disclosed recognition evaluations across users, lighting conditions and technical vocabulary, alongside correction-interface improvements.

stories.title: Borrow interface questions from forty years of style guides
stories.script: And finally, UI style guides is Marcin Wichary's newly dated collection of eighty-six preserved interface guides, stretching from the early nineteen-eighties to today. Some are PDFs, some are mirrored websites, and a few required scanning or extraction from older formats. Interface developers get a wonderfully specific library for exploring decisions that today's component libraries can make feel inevitable. There's an Amiga guide from nineteen ninety-one, preliminary BeOS guidance recovered from an installation CD, and a DECwindows guide reverse engineered from a proprietary ebook format. Wichary groups material by themes and eras and has lightly repaired some mirrors to make them easier to read. Pick one behavior you're designing, then compare how two different systems explained it to their developers. Historical guidance won't establish what works best for your users today. It can, however, give you another option to prototype. Your next settings dialog might begin with a question somebody already argued about before the web existed.
stories.why_now: The primary collection is dated November 26, 2026 and lists 86 style guides. Its Lobsters posting is timestamped November 25 at 18:54:10.835-06:00 and had 45 points and 0 comments at 2026-11-27T08:00:06.368420+00:00; the supplied page and discussion dates differ.
stories.why_early: The fresh contribution is an organized preservation collection with scans, extracted material and repaired website mirrors, rather than newly invented interface principles. Completeness, historical fidelity and the suitability of individual guidelines for present-day users are not independently established.
stories.watch_next: Additional recovered guides and practical comparisons that turn historical interface decisions into testable contemporary prototypes.
